## [Chlamydomonas - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/chlamydomonas)

# Chlamydomonas
## [Biology of Microalgae](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128114056000037)
### 6.8.2 _Chlamydomonas_ (Chlorophyta, Chlorophyceae, Chlamydomonadaceae)
_Chlamydomonas_ is a very large genus of unicellular, motile flagellates occurring in stagnant water and on damp soil, in freshwater, seawater, and even in snow. The cells have a [glycoprotein](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/glycoprotein) wall and two equal flagella. The nucleus is enclosed in a cup-shaped chloroplast, which has a single large [pyrenoid](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/pyrenoid). Two small contractile vacuoles, which have an [excretory function](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/excretion), are located near the flagella. In _[Chlamydomonas reinhardtii](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/chlamydomonas-reinhardtii)_ the reddish “eyespot” consists of two highly ordered layers of carotenoid-rich lipid globules inside the chloroplast. The outermost layer is attached to specialized areas of the chloroplast envelope membranes. This “eyespot” is thought to filter and focus the light on a [photoreceptor](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/photoreceptor) on the [plasma membrane](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/plasma-membrane) overlying the eyespot which then somehow affects the beating of the flagella (Hegemann and Berthold, 2009). The cell wall is composed of seven distinct layers with hydroxyproline-rich glycoproteins as major constituents.

The nuclear, chloroplast, and [mitochondrial genomes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/mitochondrial-genome) have been completely sequenced and extensively annotated (Blaby et al., 2014).

Vegetative cell division begins by the cells becoming immobile and losing their flagella and the flagella [basal bodies](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/basal-body) migrate towards the nucleus, and during [prophase](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/prophase) the two sets of basal bodies move to opposite ends of the nucleus. Following mitotic nuclear division, the chloroplast divides followed by cytokinesis. When all cell divisions are complete, a new cell wall forms around each daughter cell and the flagella are reformed from the basal bodies.

The haploid cells of opposite mating types (usually referred to as “plus (+)” and “minus (−)” gametes) form pairs by initially connecting at their flagella tips and mating tubes form between the flagella of each gamete accompanied by a loss of the cell wall. These cells form new cell walls and flagella and are released when the zygospore wall breaks down.

## [Microalgae for biotechnological applications: Cultivation, harvesting and biomass processing](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0044848620302246)
### 2.3 _Chlamydomonas_
_Chlamydomonas_ are unicellular [green algae](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/chlorophyta) (Chlorophyta), formed by a cell wall, chloroplast and two flagella that they use to move around (Zullaikah et al., 2019).

_Chlamydomonas_ have flagella equivalent to mammalian flagella and cilia, which distinguish them from terrestrial plants (Pazour and Witman, 2009; Silflow and Lefebvre, 2001).

## [Genomic Insights into the Biology of Algae](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123914996000062)
### 2.1 _Chlamydomonas_ is a Prototypical Volvocine Alga
#### 2.1.2 _Chlamydomonas_ Cell Structure
Each _Chlamydomonas_ cell is 5–10 _μ_ M in diameter and is shaped like a pear or ovoid (Fig. 6.3). 6.3). The flagella and basal bodies are structurally and functionally homologous to cilia and basal bodies of animal cells and _Chlamydomonas_ serves as a model for investigating these [organelles](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/organelle) (Dutcher, 2003; Pedersen & Rosenbaum, 2008). The nucleus is positioned below the basal bodies, while the posterior of each cell is occupied by a single large cup-shaped chloroplast that encompasses over half of the total cell volume (Fig. 6.3). _Chlamydomonas_ is of particular interest for evolutionary genomics because it has attributes of land plants (chloroplast, photosynthetic metabolism) and of animals, lower plants and [protists](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/protist) (flagella and basal bodies) (Grossman _et al._, 2003; Harris, 2001; Merchant _et al._, 2007).

![](https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-B9780123914996000062-f06-03-9780123914996.jpg)

Figure 6.3. Cell structure of _Chlamydomonas reinhardtii_. Schematic representation of the subcellular components of a typical _Chlamydomonas_ cell; flagella (F), basal body (B), nucleus (N), eye spot (E), golgi apparatus (G), mitochondria (M), chloroplast (C), thylakoids (T) and the pyrenoid (P). For colour version of this figure, the reader is referred to the online version of this book.

## [Phylum Protozoa](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128141144000035)
### _Chlamydomonas_
#### Morphology
A typical solitary phytomonad, its body is a [thallus](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/thallus), which consists of a single biflagellate [haploid cell](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/haploidy). The detailed internal organization of this alga is as follows:

Fig. Cell structure of _Chlamydomonas reinhardtii_, showing the central nucleus (N) with the nucleolus (Nu), the two isoform flagella (F), the cup shaped chloroplast (C) with the eye spot (E) and the starch-containing pyrenoid (P) and the mitochondria (M).

(ii)

The cytoplasm shows two distinct regions: the thin clear outer region with two anteriorly placed flagella, few strands of granular reticulum, free ribosomes, volutin granules and mitochondria; and the dense region possessing perinuclear dictosomes (Golgi complex), numerous mitochondria, free ribosomes, a few strands of granular [endoplasmic reticulum](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/endoplasmic-reticulum), a single chloroplast and a nucleus.

(iii)

The single nucleus is located centrally, sometimes near the anterior end, in the cup-shaped cavity of chloroplast, embedded in colourless cytoplasm.

A pair of whip-like flagella extend from one end, to which attaches a basal granule, the blepharoplasty, that controls the movement of the flagella. Apical and equal in length, but longer than the length of the organism, each flagellum consists of an axial thread surrounded by a sheath. Flagella exhibit synchronous movement (see Fig.

Fig. 3.3.

(v)

The single large cup-shaped, double-membraned and sac-like chloroplast occupies the greater part of the cell, and is generally parietal in position. It encloses a granular matrix (stroma), which contains ribosomes and is considered to be the site of chloroplast [protein synthesis](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/protein-synthesis).

(vi)

One or more protein [pyrenoid](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/pyrenoid) bodies, spherical in shape, usually accompany the chloroplast and are involved in starch production, and may be surrounded by [starch granules](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/starch-granule). The shape and position of the chloroplast and the number of associated pyrenoids are specific features.

The most striking structure in the organism is the red stigma, or eyespot, which lies laterally in the anterior end of the cell inside the chloroplast; it is in fact a part of the chloroplast (Fig. In [light microscopy](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/light-microscopy), it appears as a tiny orange or reddish dot. In [electron microscopy](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/electron-microscopy), it can be seen as a linear arrangement of [pigments](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/photosynthetic-pigment) associated with the chloroplast (Fig.

Fig. Bar=0.2μm.

(viii)

The organisms have no large central vacuole, but they do have one or more tiny, osmoregulatory contractile vacuoles.

## [FLAGELLATED GREEN ALGAE](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780127415505500076)
### II.DIVERSITY AND MORPHOLOGY
The [Volvocales](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/volvocales) usually have cell walls, loricae, or gelatinous matrices. Ultrastructure of the cell walls reveals their median, tripartite structure. The [vegetative cells](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/vegetative-cells) have two or sometimes four or eight equal flagella of the whiplash type at the anterior end, a single nucleus in the center, and two contractile vacuoles generally located near the base of the flagella. The chloroplasts of most species are single and cup-shaped or they may appear H-shaped, asteroid, lamellate, or be divided into discoidal units (Iyengar and Desikachary, 1981; Ettl, 1983). The chloroplast envelope consists of two layers without a chloroplast [endoplasmic reticulum](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/endoplasmic-reticulum). The [pyrenoid](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/pyrenoid) and stigma (eyespot) are generally contained within the chloroplast.

After the daughter colonies are released from the parental colony, the new colonies increase their size with their cell number unchanged. Naked unicellular species usually undergo bipartition or cell division during swimming. Although evolution from isogamy to oogamy through anisogamy can be recognized in relation to increase in colonial complexity within the colonial Volvocales (Nozaki and Ito, 1994; Kirk, 1998; Nozaki _et al._, 2002), unicellular genera such as _Chlamydomona_ s or _[Chlorogonium](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/chlorogonium)_ exhibit these three types of sexual reproduction (Ettl, 1983). However, only one of the four haploid nuclei survives to form a single gone cell in the colonial Volvocales (Volvocaceae) (Coleman, 1959; Goldstein, 1964; Nozaki _et al._, 1989).

Thus, further studies using both molecular and morphological data are needed to establish a natural taxonomic system for the flagellated [green algae](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/chlorophyta).

# [algae](https://www.britannica.com/science/algae)
## The algal cell
Algal cells are [eukaryotic](https://www.britannica.com/science/eukaryote) and contain three types of double-membrane-bound [organelles](https://www.britannica.com/science/organelle): the [nucleus](https://www.britannica.com/science/nucleus-biology), the [chloroplast](https://www.britannica.com/science/chloroplast), and the [mitochondrion](https://www.britannica.com/science/cell-biology/Regulation-of-RNA-after-synthesis#ref37413). In most algal cells there is only a single nucleus, although some cells are multinucleate. In addition, some algae are siphonaceous, meaning the many nuclei are not separated by cell walls. In all algae, the two membranes that surround the nucleus are referred to as the [nuclear envelope](https://www.britannica.com/science/nuclear-envelope). The nuclear envelope typically has specialized nuclear pores that regulate the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus.

[Chloroplasts](https://www.britannica.com/science/chloroplast) are the sites of [photosynthesis](https://www.britannica.com/science/photosynthesis), the complex set of biochemical reactions that use the energy of light to convert [carbon dioxide](https://www.britannica.com/science/carbon-dioxide) and water into sugars. Each chloroplast contains flattened, membranous sacs, called thylakoids, that contain the photosynthetic light-harvesting pigments, the [chlorophylls](https://www.britannica.com/science/chlorophyll), [carotenoids](https://www.britannica.com/science/carotenoid), and phycobiliproteins ( _see below_ [Photosynthesis](https://www.britannica.com/science/algae/Photosynthesis-and-light-absorbing-pigments#ref31721)).

Chloroplasts and mitochondria also have their own DNA. The similarity of chloroplastic and mitochondrial DNA to prokaryotic DNA has led many scientists to accept the [hypothesis](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/hypothesis) of endosymbiosis, which states that these organelles developed as a result of a long and successful symbiotic association of prokaryote cells inside eukaryote host cells.

When too much water enters the cells, contractile vacuoles serve to eject it.

The nonmembrane-bound organelles of algae include the [ribosomes](https://www.britannica.com/science/ribosome), pyrenoids, [microtubules](https://www.britannica.com/science/microtubule), and microfilaments. The [pyrenoid](https://www.britannica.com/science/pyrenoid), a [dense](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/dense) structure inside or beside chloroplasts of certain algae, consists largely of ribulose biphosphate carboxylase, one of the enzymes necessary in photosynthesis for carbon fixation and thus sugar formation. [Starch](https://www.britannica.com/science/starch), a storage form of [glucose](https://www.britannica.com/science/glucose), is often found around pyrenoids. [Microtubules,](https://www.britannica.com/science/microtubule) tubelike structures formed from tubulin proteins, are present in most cells. In many algae, microtubules appear and disappear as needed. Microtubules also provide a sort of “rail” system along which vesicles are transported. Finally, certain kinds of microtubules also form the basic structure, or [axoneme](https://www.britannica.com/science/axoneme), of a [flagellum](https://www.britannica.com/science/flagellum), and they are a major component of the [root](https://www.britannica.com/science/root-plant) system that anchors a flagellum within the cell.

# [Flagella](https://www.britannica.com/science/flagellum)
[![Take a microscopic look at how a eukaryotic flagellate's flagellum propels the organism through water](https://cdn.britannica.com/04/22004-138-0E05FFAB/Movement-flagella-motion.jpg?w=800&h=450&c=crop)](https://www.britannica.com/video/Movement-flagella-motion/-16501)

Take a microscopic look at how a eukaryotic flagellate's flagellum propels the organism through waterMovement of eukaryotic flagella in real time and slow motion.(more)

[See all videos for this article](https://www.britannica.com/science/algae/images-videos)

Each flagellum consists of an axoneme, or cylinder, with nine outer pairs of microtubules surrounding two central microtubules. The outer pairs of microtubules are connected to the axoneme by a protein called nexin. Each of the nine outer pairs of microtubules has an _a_ tubule and a _b_ tubule. The _a_ tubule has numerous molecules of a protein called dynein that are attached along its length. [Extensions](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Extensions) of dynein, called dynein arms, connect neighbouring tubules, forming dynein cross-bridges. In the presence of ATP, dynein molecules are activated, and the flagellum bends as dynein arms on one side of a dynein cross-bridge become activated and move up the microtubule. This creates the power stroke. The dynein arms on the opposite side of the dynein cross-bridge are then activated and slide up the opposite microtubule. This causes the flagellum to bend in the opposite direction during the recovery stroke.

The flagellum membrane is also complex. It may contain special receptors called chemoreceptors that respond to chemical stimuli and allow the algal cell to recognize a multitude of signals, ranging from signals carrying information about changes in the alga’s [environment](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/environment) to signals carrying information about mating partners. The flagellum membrane merges into the [cell membrane](https://www.britannica.com/science/cell-membrane), where the nine pairs of axonemal microtubules enter the main body of the cell. At this junction, each pair of microtubules is joined by an additional microtubule, forming nine triplets. This cylinder of nine triplets, [constituting](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/constituting) the [basal body](https://www.britannica.com/science/kinetosome), anchors the flagellum in the cell membrane. The anchorage provided by the basal body is strengthened by musclelike fibres and special microtubules called microtubular roots. Most [flagellate](https://www.britannica.com/science/flagellate) cells have two flagella, and therefore two basal bodies, each with microtubular roots. The orientation of the flagella and the arrangement of the musclelike fibres and microtubular roots are important taxonomic features that can be used to classify algae and are especially important in the classification of the [Chlorophyta](https://www.britannica.com/science/green-algae).

## Requirements
- Keep curated DNA content hidden until a source is on the plate and research succeeds.
- Award XP for successful lab protocols and genome sequencing; allow uncapped level progression.
- Show selected-element name, badge, description, and source; provide neutral context for elements without guide entries.

The cell is usually ovoid, has a single cup-shaped chloroplast with a pyrenoid and two contractile vacuoles at the bases of the flagella, and is surrounded with a thin cellulose wall and a thick gelatinous sheath. (ref. ID; 3490)

Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (ref. ID; 3721, 4189)
Chlamydomonas simplex (Pascher) (ref. ID; 3490)


Chlamydomonas bullosa Butcher, 1959 (ref. ID; 3721)
Descriptions

Light microscopy: Cell length ranges from 10 um to 14.4 um (average 12 um). The average width of cells is 10 um. Young cells are narrowly ovoid, becoming more broadly ovoid as they age. The cell wall is prominent but distant from the periplast, and extends to a distinct saddle-shaped papilla. The chromatophore is apple green, cup-shaped and has a narrow but deep sinus. The nucleus is easily distinguishable, being located in an anterior position in the sinus of the chromatophore. The pyrenoid is round to oval and is in the posterior half of the cell. Some cells had two pyrenoids. The elongated eyespot is in an antero-median position. The two flagella are equal to the length of the cell. In cell division up to four daughter cells are produced. (ref. ID; 3721)
Electron microscopy: The cell is bounded by a cell wall 80 nm in thickness, composed of several layers. Immediately inside the cell wall is a pitted granular layer in close proximity to the bounding membrane of the chloroplast. The thickness of this layer varies from 30 to 160 nm, and the pits are typically 100 nm in diameter. The overall thickness of the cell surface structure is 330 nm. The granular layer is an extension of the cytoplasm into the space between the chloroplast and the outer cell wall. The nucleus is roughly spherical, and typically 2.4 um in diameter. The nucleolus has a smooth regular outline, and is 1.4 um in diameter. Mitochondria are numerous throughout the cell and may be spherical, ranging in diameter from 550 to 950 nm, or elongated, reaching up to 2.7 um in length. Golgi bodies are located throughout the cell 7 to 9 saccules were observed in the stacks, which measured from 240 to 370 nm across. The saccules are flatly stacked, and a maximum of 6 golgi bodies per cell were observed. At least two are closely associated with the nucleus. The pyrenoid is spherical, posterior to median in position, and is typically 3 um in diameter. It is surrounded by a starch sheath 4 um across, which is penetrated by numerous chloroplast thylakoids with bundles of 2-4 lamellae. The chloroplast occurs in all parts of the cell, between other cell components. The intraplastidial eyespot is up to 1 um long. It consists of a double layer of pigment granules. Rough endoplasmic reticulum occurs throughout the cell. (ref. ID; 3721)


Chlamydomonas simplex (Pascher) (ref. ID; 3490)
Descriptions
The simple spherical species, 17-20 um in diameter. (ref. ID; 3490)

## Objective
- Complete and verify GENESIS’s DNA Codex, researcher progression, and periodic-table features, then make the cell graphic more realistic using real-world research.

## Requirements
- Keep curated DNA content hidden until a source is on the plate and research succeeds.
- Award XP for successful lab protocols and genome sequencing; allow uncapped level progression.
- Show selected-element name, badge, description, and source; provide neutral context for elements without guide entries.
- Let players add an element to the plate and observe a cell response.
- Present cell-mechanic connections as educational examples, not real-cell predictions; clarify that the DNA guide is curated, not exhaustive.
- Element markers are visual-only annotations, not doses, and must not alter cell metrics.
- Improve the cell graphic’s biological realism based on real-life research.

## Decisions
- Use evidence-supported educational connections; avoid unsupported reaction-specific biological claims.
- For elements without guide entries, show neutral periodic-table context.
- Element markers persist per cell and trigger a brief halo without changing cell metrics.
- Codex guides use `.codex-entry` as their selector.
- Research for more realistic anatomy focused on unicellular green algae, especially *Chlamydomonas*; relevant structures include a cell wall, cup-shaped chloroplast, nucleus, pyrenoid, contractile vacuoles, eyespot, and flagella.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented cell mechanics, Codex access gating, researcher progression, 118 periodic-table elements, and per-cell element markers.
- Verified fresh locked state, responsive plate and periodic table, sourced element details, neutral context for helium, marker persistence and cell isolation, and unchanged cell metrics.
- Verified successful lab protocol and sequencing XP, unlocked Codex visibility with all 13 guides, and progression beyond level 40.
- Confirmed no uncaught browser exceptions; removed the isolated test save and verified local and session storage were empty.
- `node --check app.js` and `git diff --check` passed.

### Active
- Update the existing cell illustration to look more biologically realistic, informed by the researched microalgal anatomy.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect the existing organism markup and styles, then implement a more research-informed cell illustration while preserving the project’s visual style.
2. Verify the updated graphic in the browser and run relevant checks.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Simulation state and organism markup, including the `.cell-visual` illustration.
- `style.css`: Current `.cell-visual` and related illustration styles.
- `index.html`: Navigation and researcher-progress markup.
- `genesis-latest.jpeg`: Updated observatory screenshot.

## Important Context
- Existing changes are uncommitted in `app.js`, `style.css`, `index.html`, and `genesis-latest.jpeg`.
- Persistence key: `genesis-living-genome-v1`; test storage was cleared.
- `recordResearchSuccess` requires 100 XP to advance from level 1; after two successes the expected state is level 2 with 100 XP, not level 3.
- Biological reference found: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/chlamydomonas-reinhardtii

<subagent sessionID="ses_e4673ee49ffecPo2s3mlMCf5ld" state="completed">
## Existing plate model and insertion points

The plate is an array of cell records in `S.plate`. Its initial contents are created by `makePlateState()` (`app.js:48`), and `addCellsToPlate()` (`app.js:84`) creates additional records. Both constructors assume a **cell**: each record has cell metrics such as viability, ATP, membrane integrity, and cycle progress, along with a `genomeId`.

- **Preset data:** Add the five preset definitions near the existing genome/state setup in `app.js`, and connect each preset to a cell-creation path. `plateGenome()` (`app.js:82`) resolves a plate item’s genome from `S.plateSources`, the archive, or the active genome.
- **Controls:** `cellView()` (`app.js:87`) builds the observatory controls. It already includes “Add live cells” and “Advance cell cycle”; `handleAction()` (`app.js:117`) handles those actions and an existing `plate-archive` action. A preset selector or buttons would need corresponding action handling there.
- **Rendering and selection:** `plateCellMarkup()` (`app.js:83`) creates the selectable plate items. The delegated click listener (`app.js:118`) handles `[data-plate-cell]` selection and `[data-action]` actions.
- **Simulation updates:** `advancePlateCells()` (`app.js:64`) applies cell physiology and cycle progression; `dividePlateCell()` (`app.js:63`) creates dividing daughter cells.
- **Persistence:** `storeState()`/`loadState()` use `genesis-living-genome-v1` (`app.js:3, 50–53`). Plate data and its `plateSources` are part of saved state; startup normalization in `app.js:53` fills missing cell fields.

## Styling

The plate appearance is chiefly defined by `.plate-stage`, `.plate-dish`, `.plate-cell`, and `.plate-cell-body` in `style.css:3`. `plateCellMarkup()` sets CSS custom properties such as `--cell-hue`, `--cell-size`, and `--cell-speed`, which those rules use. The overview’s `.organism-art` and `.cell-visual` styles are potential references for a separate, non-plate schematic.

## Key risks

1. **The requested presets are not all cells.** Rat, bird, and tuna can be represented as host-cell presets, but flu and HIV are viruses. The current model gives every plate item cellular structures, cell-cycle progression, and division. Treating viruses as ordinary cells would be biologically misleading; distinguish virus particles from host cells and model their lifecycle separately, or clearly label them as simplified representations.
2. **The renderer and inspector imply cell anatomy.** `plateCellMarkup()` always draws a nucleus and organelles, while `cellView()` presents a list of cellular components. Adding viruses without a distinct visual and inspection mode would preserve those cell-specific assumptions.
3. **The simulation advances and divides every plate entry.** `advancePlateCells()` updates cell metrics and can trigger division through `dividePlateCell()`. A viral preset needs an explicit rule to bypass or replace those mechanics.
4. **Plate capacity is capped at 30.** `addCellsToPlate()` limits additions to the remaining slots, and `dividePlateCell()` refuses division at the cap (`app.js:63–64, 84`). Five presets should account for that limit.
5. **Saved state needs a migration/normalization plan.** Existing plate records are persisted locally. New preset fields or item types should be initialized safely for previously saved records in the startup normalization block (`app.js:53`); changing the storage key would instead start a separate saved state.
6. **Genome compatibility matters.** `plateGenome()` and downstream trait calculations expect the existing genome shape. Preset records should either provide compatible genome data or use an explicit alternate model path, rather than assuming a virus can be treated as a cell genome unchanged.

Files reviewed: [`/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/app.js`](/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/app.js) and [`/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/style.css`](/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/style.css). No files were modified.
</subagent>

## [Red blood cell - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell)

## Structure
### Vertebrates
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Erythrocytes_in_vertebrates.jpg/250px-Erythrocytes_in_vertebrates.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Erythrocytes_in_vertebrates.jpg) There is an immense size variation in vertebrate red blood cells, as well as a correlation between cell and nucleus size. Mammalian red blood cells, which do not contain nuclei, are considerably smaller than those of most other vertebrates. [[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-Gulliver1875-10)[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Cytological_abnormalities_in_peripheral_blood_erythrocytes_of_penguins_Pygoscelis_papua_5.jpg/250px-Cytological_abnormalities_in_peripheral_blood_erythrocytes_of_penguins_Pygoscelis_papua_5.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cytological_abnormalities_in_peripheral_blood_erythrocytes_of_penguins_Pygoscelis_papua_5.jpg) Mature red blood cells of birds have a nucleus, however in the blood of adult females of penguin _[Pygoscelis papua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentoo_penguin)_ enucleated red blood cells ( **B**) have been observed, but with very low frequency.

The vast majority of vertebrates, including [mammals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal) and humans, have red blood cells. These erythrocytes are cells present in blood to transport oxygen. The only known vertebrates without red blood cells are the crocodile icefish (family [Channichthyidae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channichthyidae)); they live in very oxygen-rich cold water and transport oxygen freely dissolved in their blood. [[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-11) While they no longer use hemoglobin, remnants of hemoglobin genes can be found in their [genome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome). [[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-12)

Oxygen can easily [diffuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffusion) through the erythrocyte's [cell membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_membrane). [[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-13)

The color of red blood cells is due to the heme group of hemoglobin. _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)_]

The size of red blood cells varies widely among vertebrate species; red blood cell width is on average about 25% larger than [capillary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capillary) diameter, and it has been hypothesized that this improves the oxygen transfer from red blood cells to tissues. [[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-snyder-15)

### Mammals
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Gray453.png/330px-Gray453.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gray453.png) Typical mammalian red blood cells: (a) seen from surface; (b) in profile, forming rouleaux; (c) rendered spherical by water; (d) rendered crenate (shrunken and spiky) by salt. (c) and (d) do not normally occur in the body. The last two shapes are due to water being transported into, and out of, the cells, by [osmosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osmosis).

The red blood cells of [mammals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal) are typically shaped as biconcave disks: flattened and depressed in the center, with a [dumbbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumbbell)-shaped cross section, and a [torus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torus)-shaped rim on the edge of the disk. Members of this order have clearly evolved a mode of red blood cell development substantially different from the mammalian norm. [[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-Gulliver1875-10)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-The_bigger_the_C-value,_the_larger-17) Overall, mammalian red blood cells are remarkably flexible and deformable so as to squeeze through tiny [capillaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capillary), as well as to maximize their apposing surface by assuming a cigar shape, where they efficiently release their oxygen load. [[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-18)

Red blood cells in mammals are unique amongst vertebrates as most species [do not have nuclei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enucleation_(microbiology)) when mature. [[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-19) They do have nuclei during early phases of [erythropoiesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoiesis), but extrude them during development as they mature; this provides more space for hemoglobin. The red blood cells without nuclei, called [reticulocytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reticulocytes), subsequently lose all other cellular [organelles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organelle) such as their [mitochondria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrion), [Golgi apparatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golgi_apparatus) and [endoplasmic reticulum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endoplasmic_reticulum).

In some other mammals such as dogs and horses, the spleen sequesters large numbers of red blood cells, which are dumped into the blood during times of exertion stress, yielding a higher oxygen transport capacity.

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Red_White_Blood_cells.jpg/250px-Red_White_Blood_cells.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Red_White_Blood_cells.jpg) Scanning electron micrograph of blood cells. From left to right: human red blood cell, [thrombocyte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platelet) (platelet), [leukocyte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leukocyte).

## Microstructure
### Nucleus
Red blood cells in mammals are _anucleate_ when mature, meaning that they lack a [cell nucleus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_nucleus). In comparison, the red blood cells of other vertebrates have nuclei; the only known exceptions are [salamanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salamander) of the family _[Plethodontidae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plethodontidae)_, where five different clades has evolved various degrees of enucleated red blood cells (most evolved in some species of the genus _[Batrachoseps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batrachoseps)_), and fish of the genus _[Maurolicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurolicus)_. [[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-28)

[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_blood_cell#cite_note-The_bigger_the_C-value,_the_larger-17) The argument runs as follows: Efficient gas transport requires red blood cells to pass through very narrow capillaries, and this constrains their size.

[Nucleated red blood cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleated_red_blood_cell) in mammals consist of two forms: normoblasts, which are normal erythropoietic precursors to mature red blood cells, and megaloblasts, which are abnormally large precursors that occur in [megaloblastic anemias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megaloblastic_anemia).

## [Red Blood Cells in Animals - Circulatory System](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/hematopoietic-system-introduction/red-blood-cells-in-animals)

# Red Blood Cells in Animals
- [Key Points](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/hematopoietic-system-introduction/red-blood-cells-in-animals#Key-Points_v43545986) |
- [For More Information](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/hematopoietic-system-introduction/red-blood-cells-in-animals#For-More-Information_v43545995) |

Erythrocytes (RBCs) are largely produced from hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow.

In most mammals, mature RBCs have a biconcave disk shape and lack a nucleus. Nucleated red blood cells (nRBCs), or erythroblasts, are immature RBCs that have not undergone nuclear extrusion and still contain a nucleus. Camelid RBCs are elliptical. Mature RBCs in birds are large oval cells containing oval nuclei.

This process requires the following biological elements:

Interference with synthesis or release of Hgb, production or survival of RBCs, or metabolism can cause disease.

Hgb is a complex molecule, formed of 4 heme units attached to 4 globins (2 alpha and 2 beta globins).

In these diseases, production of globins (alpha, beta, or both) does not balance heme production, and Hgb is not functional.

RBC mass, and thus oxygen-carrying capacity, remains constant over time in healthy animals.

Once produced in bone marrow, mature RBCs have a finite lifespan in circulation before senescent RBCs are destroyed. RBC production and destruction must be carefully balanced to avoid both anemia and [erythrocytosis](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/erythrocytosis-polycythemia/erythrocytosis-polycythemia-in-animals) (excess RBCs in circulation).

Erythropoiesis (RBC production) is regulated by **erythropoietin**, a hormone that increases in the presence of hypoxia. Erythropoietin acts on bone marrow in concert with other humoral mediators to increase the number of stem cells entering RBC production, shorten maturation time, and cause early release of reticulocytes (immature RBCs).

Toxic insult, infectious diseases (eg, [feline leukemia virus disease](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/infectious-diseases/feline-leukemia-virus/feline-leukemia-virus-disease), [histoplasmosis](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/infectious-diseases/fungal-infections/histoplasmosis-in-animals)), and neoplasms within bone marrow (eg, [myelofibrosis](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/anemia/nonregenerative-anemias-in-animals#v92095905)) can all primarily affect the bone marrow, leading to decreased erythropoiesis with or without other cytopenias.

Both conserve the principal constituents of the cell for reuse.

As RBCs age, they change antigenically, acquiring senescent antigens and losing flexibility because of impaired ATP production.

After phagocytosis and subsequent disruption of the cell membrane, Hgb is converted to heme and globin. Iron is released from the heme moiety and either stored in the macrophage as ferritin or hemosiderin or released into the circulation for transport back to the marrow. The remaining heme is converted to bilirubin, which is released by macrophages into the systemic circulation, where it complexes with albumin for transport to hepatocytes. In the liver, it is conjugated and excreted into the bile.

In diseases causing excess extravascular hemolysis, RBCs may be destroyed before they are senescent, resulting in a shortened RBC lifespan, anemia, and hyperbilirubinemia.

The energy of ATP is used to fuel RBC membrane pumps that work to preserve cell shape and flexibility.

The reducing potential of NADH is utilized via the methemoglobin reductase pathway to maintain iron in Hgb in its reduced form (Fe2+).

Inherited deficiency of pyruvate kinase, a key glycolytic enzyme, causes ATP deficiency, which leads to decreased RBC lifespan and hemolytic anemia.

**Relative erythrocytosis** is the term used to describe increased RBC mass relative to plasma, which most commonly results from dehydration (hemoconcentration) or splenic contraction.

## For More Information

## [THE BIOLOGY OF INFLUENZA VIRUSES - PMC - NIH](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/)

# THE BIOLOGY OF INFLUENZA VIRUSES
[Nicole M Bouvier](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=%22Bouvier%20NM%22[Author])

## Abstract
The influenza viruses are characterized by segmented, negative-strand RNA genomes requiring an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase of viral origin for replication. The particular structure of the influenza virus genome and function of its viral proteins enable _antigenic drift_ and _antigenic shift_. These processes result in viruses able to evade the long-term adaptive immune responses in many hosts.

## 1. THE INFLUENZA VIRUSES
The influenza A, B, and C viruses, representing three of the five genera of the family _Orthomyxoviridae_, are characterized by segmented, negative-strand RNA genomes. Sequencing has confirmed that these viruses share a common genetic ancestry; however, they have genetically diverged, such that reassortment – the exchange of viral RNA segments between viruses – has been reported to occur within each genus, or _type_, but not across types. Influenza A viruses are further characterized by the _subtype_ of their surface glycoproteins, the hemagglutinin (HA) and the neuraminidase (NA). Thus, A/Panama/2007/1999(H3N2) was isolate number 2007 of a human influenza A virus taken in the country of Panama in 1999, and it has an HA subtype 3 and an NA subtype 2. While many genetically distinct subtypes – 16 for HA and 9 for NA – have been found in circulating influenza A viruses, only three HA (H1, H2, and H3) and two NA (N1 and N2) subtypes have caused human epidemics, as defined by sustained, widespread, person-to-person transmission [ [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R1)].

## 2. VIRION STRUCTURE AND ORGANIZATION
By electron microscopy, influenza A and B viruses are virtually indistinguishable. They are spherical or filamentous in shape, with the spherical forms on the order of 100 nm in diameter and the filamentous forms often in excess of 300 nm in length. The influenza A virion is studded with glycoprotein spikes of HA and NA, in a ratio of approximately four to one, projecting from a host cell–derived lipid membrane [ [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R1)]. A smaller number of matrix (M2) ion channels traverse the lipid envelope, with an M2:HA ratio on the order of one M2 channel per 101-102 HA molecules [ [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R2)]. The envelope and its three integral membrane proteins HA, NA, and M2 overlay a matrix of M1 protein, which encloses the virion core. Internal to the M1 matrix are found the nuclear export protein (NEP; also called nonstructural protein 2, NS2) and the ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex, which consists of the viral RNA segments coated with nucleoprotein (NP) and the heterotrimeric RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, composed of two “polymerase basic” and one “polymerase acidic” subunits (PB1, PB2, and PA). The organization of the influenza B virion is similar, with four envelope proteins: HA, NA, and, instead of M2, NB and BM2. Influenza C virions are structurally distinct from those of the A and B viruses; on infected cell surfaces, they can form long cordlike structures on the order of 500 μm. However, influenza C virions are compositionally similar, with a glycoprotein-studded lipid envelope overlying a protein matrix and the RNP complex. The influenza C viruses have only one major surface glycoprotein, the hemagglutinin-esterase-fusion (HEF) protein, which corresponds functionally to the HA and NA of influenza A and B viruses, and one minor envelope protein, CM2 [ [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R1)].

## 3. GENOME STRUCTURE
The influenza A and B virus genomes each comprise eight negative-sense, single-stranded viral RNA (vRNA) segments, while influenza C virus has a seven-segment genome. (See [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#T1).) The eight segments of influenza A and B viruses (and the seven segments of influenza C virus) are numbered in order of decreasing length. In influenza A and B viruses, segments 1, 3, 4, and 5 encode just one protein per segment: the PB2, PA, HA and NP proteins. All influenza viruses encode the polymerase subunit PB1 on segment 2; in some strains of influenza A virus, this segment also codes for the accessory protein PB1-F2, a small, 87-amino acid protein with pro-apoptotic activity, in a +1 alternate reading frame [ [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R3)]. No analogue to PB1-F2 has been identified in influenza B or C viruses. Conversely, segment 6 of the influenza A virus encodes only the NA protein, while that of influenza B virus encodes both the NA protein and, in a −1 alternate reading frame, the NB matrix protein, which is an integral membrane protein corresponding to the influenza A virus M2 protein [ [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R4)]. Segment 7 of both influenza A and B viruses code for the M1 matrix protein. In the influenza A genome, the M2 ion channel is also expressed from segment 7 by RNA splicing [ [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R5)], while influenza B virus encodes its BM2 membrane protein in a +2 alternate reading frame [ [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R6), [7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R7)]. Finally, both influenza A and B viruses possess a single RNA segment, segment 8, from which they express the interferon-antagonist NS1 protein [ [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R8)– [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R10)] and, by mRNA splicing, the NEP/NS2 [ [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R11), [12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R12)], which is involved in viral RNP export from the host cell nucleus. The genomic organization of influenza C viruses is generally similar to that of influenza A and B viruses; however, the HEF protein of influenza C replaces the HA and NA proteins, and thus the influenza C virus genome has one fewer segment than that of influenza A or B viruses.

### TABLE 1. The genomic segments of influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (H1N1) virus and their encoded proteins.
[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/table/T1/)

The ends of each vRNA segment form a helical hairpin, which is bound by the heterotrimeric RNA polymerase complex; the remainder of the segment is coated with arginine-rich NP, the net positive charge of which binds the negatively charged phosphate backbone of the vRNA [ [13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R13)– [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R15)]. Each vRNA segment possesses noncoding regions, of varying lengths, at both 3′ and 5′ ends. However, the extreme ends of all segments are highly conserved among all influenza virus segments; these partially complementary termini base-pair to function as the promoter for vRNA replication and transcription by the viral polymerase complex. The noncoding regions also include the mRNA polyadenylation signal and part of the packaging signals for virus assembly.

A segmented genome enables _antigenic shift_, in which an influenza A virus strain acquires the HA segment, and possibly the NA segment as well, from an influenza virus of a different subtype. This segment reassortment can happen in cells infected with different human and animal viruses, and the resulting virus may encode completely novel antigenic proteins to which the human population has no preexisting immunity. Pandemic influenza arises when antigenic shift generates a virus to which humans are susceptible but immunologically naïve. Antigenic shift likely produced the influenza A (H1N1) virus that was the causative agent of the 1918–1919 “Spanish flu,” whose lethality was unparalleled in modern times. Characterization of the reconstructed 1918 influenza virus indicated that its unique constellation of genes was responsible for its extreme virulence, with the HA, NA, and PB1 genes all contributing to its high pathogenicity [ [16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R16), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R17)]. The global spread of the pandemic was almost certainly enabled by the acquisition of antigenically novel surface proteins, to which much of the world’s population was immunologically naïve [ [18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/#R18)].

# Influenza Virus: A Brief Overview
## Introduction
### Table 1.
Properties of the subtypes of influenza virus

| Properties | A | B | C |
|-|-|-|-|
| Occurrence | Most frequent | Very low | Rare |
| Severity | Virulent | Mild | Not virulent |
| Outbreaks | Pandemic/epidemic [ [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR6)] | Epidemic [ [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR6)] | Sporadic [ [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR6)] |
| Mutation & recombination rate | High (antigenic shift and antigenic drift) | Low (only antigenic drift) | No recombination |
| Reservoir | Wild aquatic bird | No | No |
| Host range | Wide (Human, Birds, Horse, Pig, Ferret, mice) | Limited to human | Only in humans |
| Subtypes | Many with different combination of 16 HA & 9 NA | No subtypes | No subtypes |
| RNA genome | Consist of eight segments | Eight segments | Seven segments |

## Influenza Virus
All three subtypes of influenza virus (A, B, C) are similar in structure but vary antigenically. Influenza viruses are about 80–120 nm in size, roughly spherical/ovoid in shape. All contain single-stranded, negative-sense, segmented RNA genome (having eight segments of variable length). These encodes 11 proteins including nine structural [Polymerase proteins—polymerase basic protein 1 (PB1), PB1-F2, PB2 and polymerase acidic protein (PA), surface glycoproteins—haemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA), Nucleocapsid protein—nucleoproteins (NP), Matrix proteins—M1, Ion pore protein—M2] and two nonstructural proteins (NS1 and NS2) respectively [ [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR8)].

Structurally, virus is enclosed by outermost envelope made up of lipid bilayer from host membrane that consists of two surface glycoproteins, HA and NA which act as antigenic determinants and induce humoral immune response in host (Fig. [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#Fig1)). HA is mainly responsible for virus attachment to target cells and entry of viral genome into the host cell while NA participates in release of progeny virus particles from infected host cells by cleaving terminal sialic acid residue on host cell surface. Influenza A virus is classified into subtypes on the basis of these surface glycoproteins. To date, 16 serologically distinct HA and 9 NA have been identified and are sequentially named as H1, H2, H3 and so on and N1, N2……etc. Currently, H1, H2 and H3 in combination with N1 and N2 are most frequently circulating types in human. Remaining subtypes remain to be zoonotic, causing disease mainly in fowl and nonhuman primates [ [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR5), [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR6)]. Viral proteins encoded by segmented RNA genome have various functions biological as well as in pathogenesis during infection. The three largest RNA segments encode proteins PA, PB1 and PB2, jointly act as a RNA dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP). PB1 gene segment also encode small 87 residue nonstructural protein PB1-F2 having apoptotic function [ [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR9)]. Surface proteins HA, NA and NP are encoded by intermediate sized RNA segments. Remaining RNA segments encode M1 matrix protein and M2 ion pore protein. Two nonstructural proteins NS1A and NS2/NEP are encoded by very small RNA segments, functions of all these proteins are shown in Table [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#Tab2). Influenza virus make entry into host by attachment to surface glycoproteins containing sialic acid residue on host respiratory epithelium cells with help of viral surface HA protein as shown in Fig. [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#Fig2). To date, human influenza viruses isolated from 1957 and 1968 pandemics and recent pandemic swine origin influenza virus A (SO-IVA) H1N1 virus preferentially bind to cell-surface glycoproteins or glycolipids containing terminal 2-6 linked sialyl-galactosyl moieties [Neu5Ac(α2-6)Gal] while Avian influenza virus prefer α2-3 linked glycan sialic acid [Neu5Ac(@2-3)Gal] [ [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR10)]. Recent studies depict that pandemic 2009 H1N1 (SO-IVA) virus is well adapted to mammalian hosts and binds to both α2,6-linked and α2,3-linked cellular receptors, which are present in conjunctiva, distal airways, and alveolar pneumocytes [ [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR11)]. The viral HA molecules found in the form of trimers play another role in release of viral ribo-nucleoprotein particles (vRNP) into the cytoplasm [ [12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR12)]. The HA precursor (HA0) contains two domain, one sialic acid receptor binding domain (HA1) and remaining ectodomain (HA2) also called as fusion peptide, both linked by disulfide linkage. Virus is internalized within endosome through the mechanism of receptor mediated endocytosis. After internalization, M2 viral protein (Ion channel protein) play role in acidification of endosome by enhancing proton transport from cytoplasm. Hence, acidification of the endosomes facilitate irreversible conformational changes in HA leads to dissociation of HA1 from the endosomal membrane and enable HA2, a fusion peptide to attach to the endosomal membrane. All this process initiates the fusion of the viral and endosomal membranes, resulting in the release of the RNP into the cytoplasm [ [13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR13), [14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7101909/#CR14)].

# Types of Influenza Viruses
## Influenza virus basics
A pandemic can occur when a new and different influenza A virus emerges that infects people, can spread efficiently among people, and against which people have little or no immunity. Influenza C virus infections generally cause mild illness and are not thought to cause human epidemics.

[View Larger](https://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/viruses-types.html#)

![3D View - Sliced with Key - Multiple Colors](https://www.cdc.gov/flu-resources/media/files/2024/07/3d-influenza-multicoror-key-pieslice-600px.jpg)

This is a picture of an influenza (flu) A virus.

Show More

Reassortment is when influenza viruses swap gene segments. It can occur when two different subtypes of influenza viruses infect a host at the same time and swap genetic information. Current subtypes of influenza A viruses that routinely circulate in people include A(H1N1) and A(H3N2).

[View Larger](https://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/viruses-types.html#)

![Human Seasonal Influenza Virus](https://www.cdc.gov/flu/media/images/2024/09/influenza-viruses-1200px.jpg)

Show More

## Clades and sub-clades
Other gene segments also can be broken into clades and sub-clades.

![figure 1 - phylogenetic tree , node common acestor, subclade, clade](https://www.cdc.gov/flu/media/images/2024/09/phylogenic-tree-600.jpg)

Show More

As previously described, influenza viruses have hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) surface proteins. Antigens are molecular structures/proteins on the surface of viruses that are recognized by the immune system and can trigger an immune response (such as antibody production).

## Influenza A(H1N1) viruses
Currently circulating influenza A(H1N1) viruses are descendants of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus that emerged in the spring of 2009 and caused a flu pandemic ( [CDC 2009 H1N1 Flu website](https://archive.cdc.gov/#/details?url=https://www.cdc.gov/h1n1flu/index.htm)).

- Complete and verify GENESIS’s DNA Codex, researcher progression, and periodic-table features, and improve the cell graphic’s biological realism based on real-world research.

## Requirements
- Keep curated DNA content hidden until a source is on the plate and research succeeds.
- Award XP for successful lab protocols and genome sequencing; allow uncapped level progression.
- Show selected-element name, badge, description, and source; provide neutral context for elements without guide entries.
- Let players add an element to the plate and observe a cell response.

## Objective
- Extend GENESIS’s seeded plate with five research-informed presets: rat, bird, flu, tuna, and HIV (“vih”), with realistic educational responses to plate contents.

## Requirements
- Use real-world research to inform the presets and their responses.
- Include the five requested entries in the plate.

## Decisions
- Treat them as five selectable plate presets; flu and HIV are viruses, not cells.
- Earlier cell/Codex/periodic-table requirements and decisions remain in effect, including educational framing and not presenting schematic mechanics as real-cell predictions.

## Work State
### Completed
- Existing DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and *Chlamydomonas*-inspired cell schematic were implemented and verified, as recorded in the prior checkpoint.
- Inspected plate simulation structure and gathered initial research references on mammalian versus bird/fish red blood cells and influenza virus biology.

### Active
- Design and implement the five presets, their visual representations, and research-informed plate responses.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect the remaining plate rendering, simulation update, and content-response code in `app.js`.
2. Define accurate educational distinctions for rat, bird, and tuna cell presets and non-cellular flu/HIV virus presets.
3. Implement preset selection and responses, then verify behavior and clearly label simplified or illustrative mechanics.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Plate state, cell creation, rendering, and interaction handling.
- `style.css`: Plate and cell visualization styling.

## Important Context
- Plate state is an array in `S.plate`; `makePlateState()` seeds cells, `addCellsToPlate()` adds them, `plateGenome()` resolves genomes, `plateCellMarkup()` renders cells, and `handleAction()` handles interactions.
- Initial research result: mature mammalian red blood cells lack a nucleus, while bird and fish red blood cells retain one; influenza viruses are non-cellular and have segmented negative-strand RNA.
- Research links: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2263/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/
- Changes from the earlier work remain uncommitted in `app.js`, `style.css`, `index.html`, and `genesis-latest.jpeg`; no changes for the new presets have been made yet.

The mature red blood cells of birds, fish, amphibians, and most reptiles retain their nuclei, and in some species, they also retain organelles such as ...

## [Immune functions of avian erythrocytes: a comprehensive ...](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1675279/full)

# Immune functions of avian erythrocytes: a comprehensive review from basic biology to pathogen-induced responses
## 3 Structure and molecular of avian erythrocytes
### 3.1 Structure of avain erythrocytes
#### 3.1.1 Cell nucleus
Mature avian erythrocytes possess an intermediate diameter, larger than that of mammalian erythrocytes but smaller than that of amphibian erythrocytes (13). The presence of the nucleus not only facilitates the transcription and translation of proteins essential for gas exchange but also supports the expression of proteins involved in immune responses.

## References
- [Google Scholar](http://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?author=V.%2BChico&author=I.%2BNombela&author=S.%2BPuente-Mar%C3%ADn&author=M.%2BOrtega-Villaizan&publication_year=2018&title=Nucleated%2Bred%2Bblood%2Bcells%2Bcontribute%2Bto%2Bthe%2Bhost%2Bimmune%2Bresponse%2Bagainst%2Bpathogens&journal=IntechOpen&volume=1&pages=39-60)

Prognostic value of nucleated red blood cells in critically ill children.

## [Nucleated RBC | eClinpath](https://eclinpath.com/hematology/morphologic-features/red-blood-cells/nucleated-rbcs/)

[Skip to content](https://eclinpath.com/hematology/morphologic-features/red-blood-cells/nucleated-rbcs/#content)

Nucleated RBC are usually not seen in the blood of healthy mammals (low numbers may be seen in dogs and camelids, but are rarely normally seen in other species). ## Objective
- Extend GENESIS’s seeded plate with five research-informed presets: rat, bird, flu, tuna, and HIV (“vih”), with realistic educational responses to plate contents.

## Requirements
- Use real-world research to inform the presets and their responses.
- Include all five requested entries as selectable plate presets.
- Preserve earlier DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and *Chlamydomonas*-inspired cell schematic work and educational framing.

## Decisions
- Flu and HIV are viruses, not cells; represent them distinctly from cellular presets.
- Clearly label schematic mechanics as illustrative, not as real-cell predictions.

## Work State
### Completed
- Earlier DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and cell schematic were implemented and verified.
- Inspected plate state creation and cell-addition code; gathered initial research on blood-cell differences and influenza biology.

### Active
- Design and implement the five presets, their visual representations, and research-informed plate responses.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining plate rendering, simulation update, and content-response code in `app.js`.
2. Define accurate educational distinctions for rat, bird, and tuna cell presets and non-cellular flu/HIV virus presets.
3. Implement preset selection and responses, then verify behavior and label simplified or illustrative mechanics.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Plate state, cell creation, rendering, and interaction handling.
- `style.css`: Plate and cell visualization styling.
- `index.html`: Existing interface structure, potentially relevant for adding preset controls.

## Important Context
- Plate state is stored in `S.plate`; `makePlateState()` seeds cells, `addCellsToPlate()` adds them, `plateGenome()` resolves genomes, `plateCellMarkup()` renders cells, and `handleAction()` handles interactions.
- Mature mammalian red blood cells lack nuclei, while bird and fish red blood cells retain nuclei; influenza viruses are non-cellular and have segmented negative-strand RNA.
- Research references: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2263/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/
- Changes from earlier work remain uncommitted in `app.js`, `style.css`, `index.html`, and `genesis-latest.jpeg`; no changes for the new presets have been made.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Extend GENESIS’s seeded plate with five research-informed presets: rat, bird, flu, tuna, and HIV (“vih”), with realistic educational responses to plate contents.

## Requirements
- Use real-world research to inform the presets and responses.
- Include all five requested entries as selectable plate presets.
- Preserve the existing DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and *Chlamydomonas*-inspired cell schematic work and educational framing.

## Decisions
- Flu and HIV are viruses, not cells; represent them distinctly from cellular presets.
- Label schematic mechanics as illustrative, not as real-cell predictions.

## Work State
### Completed
- Earlier DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and cell schematic were implemented and verified.
- Inspected plate state creation and cell-addition code; gathered research on blood-cell differences, influenza biology, and HIV.

### Active
- Design and implement five plate presets, visual representations, and research-informed responses.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining plate rendering, simulation update, and content-response code in `app.js`.
2. Define accurate educational distinctions for rat, bird, and tuna cell presets and non-cellular flu/HIV virus presets.
3. Implement preset selection and responses, then verify behavior and label simplified or illustrative mechanics.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Plate state, cell creation, rendering, and interaction handling.
- `style.css`: Plate and cell visualization styling.
- `index.html`: Interface structure, potentially relevant for preset controls.

## Important Context
- Plate state is stored in `S.plate`; `makePlateState()` seeds cells, `addCellsToPlate()` adds them, `plateGenome()` resolves genomes, `plateCellMarkup()` renders cells, and `handleAction()` handles interactions.
- Mature mammalian red blood cells lack nuclei; bird and fish red blood cells retain nuclei.
- Influenza A and B have eight negative-sense single-stranded RNA segments; HIV infects CD4 T lymphocytes and uses reverse transcriptase.
- Research references: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2263/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/, https://hivinfo.nih.gov/understanding-hiv/fact-sheets/hiv-life-cycle
- Existing changes remain uncommitted in `app.js`, `style.css`, `index.html`, and `genesis-latest.jpeg`; no changes for the new presets have been made.

- Preserve the existing DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and *Chlamydomonas*-inspired cell schematic.

## Requirements
- Include all five requested entries as selectable plate presets.
- Use real-world research to inform the presets and responses.
- Keep educational framing and label simplified schematic mechanics as illustrative.

## Decisions
- Flu and HIV are viruses, not cells, so represent them distinctly from cellular presets.
- Mature mammalian red blood cells lack nuclei; bird and fish red blood cells retain nuclei.

## Work State
### Completed
- DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and cell schematic were implemented and verified earlier.
- Inspected plate state creation and cell-addition code; gathered research on blood-cell differences, influenza biology, and HIV.

### Active

- (none)

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Extend GENESIS’s seeded plate with research-informed rat, bird, flu, tuna, and HIV (“vih”) presets and educational responses.

## Requirements
- Make all five entries selectable as plate presets.
- Use real-world research to inform the presets and responses.
- Keep the educational framing and identify simplified schematic mechanics as illustrative.
- Preserve the DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and *Chlamydomonas*-inspired cell schematic.

## Decisions
- Flu and HIV are viruses, not cells, so represent them distinctly from cellular presets.
- Mature mammalian red blood cells lack nuclei; bird and fish red blood cells retain nuclei.

## Work State
### Completed
- DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and cell schematic were implemented and verified earlier.
- Inspected plate state creation and cell-addition code; gathered research on blood-cell differences, influenza biology, and HIV.

### Active
- Design and implement five plate presets, visual representations, and research-informed responses.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining plate rendering, simulation update, and content-response code in `app.js`.
2. Define accurate educational distinctions for rat, bird, and tuna cell presets and non-cellular flu/HIV virus presets.
3. Implement preset selection and responses, then verify behavior and label simplified or illustrative mechanics.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Plate state, cell creation, rendering, and interaction handling.
- `style.css`: Plate and cell visualization styling.
- `index.html`: Interface structure and potentially relevant preset controls.

## Important Context
- Plate state is stored in `S.plate`; `makePlateState()` seeds cells, `addCellsToPlate()` adds them, `plateGenome()` resolves genomes, `plateCellMarkup()` renders cells, and `handleAction()` handles interactions.
- Influenza A and B have eight negative-sense single-stranded RNA segments; HIV infects CD4 T lymphocytes and uses reverse transcriptase.
- Research references: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2263/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/, https://hivinfo.nih.gov/understanding-hiv/fact-sheets/hiv-life-cycle, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4483285/
- Existing changes remain uncommitted in `app.js`, `style.css`, `index.html`, and `genesis-latest.jpeg`; no changes for the new presets have been made.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Extend GENESIS’s seeded plate with research-informed rat, bird, flu, tuna, and HIV (“vih”) presets and educational responses.

## Requirements
- Make all five entries selectable as plate presets and base their responses on real-world research.
- Preserve educational framing; label simplified schematic mechanics as illustrative.
- Preserve the DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and *Chlamydomonas*-inspired cell schematic.

## Decisions
- Flu and HIV are viruses, not cells, and should be represented distinctly from cellular presets.
- Mature mammalian red blood cells lack nuclei; bird and fish red blood cells retain nuclei.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected plate state creation, cell rendering, and action handling in `app.js`; identified insertion points for presets and responses.
- Earlier work on the DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and cell schematic was implemented and verified.

### Active
- Design and implement five selectable presets, their visual representations, and research-informed educational responses.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Define accurate educational distinctions for rat, bird, and tuna cell presets and non-cellular flu/HIV virus presets.
2. Implement preset selection, visuals, and educational responses in `app.js`, `style.css`, and possibly `index.html`.
3. Verify behavior and ensure simplified or illustrative mechanics are clearly labeled.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Plate state, cell creation/rendering, cell observatory, and `handleAction()` interactions.
- `style.css`: Plate and cell visualization styles.
- `index.html`: Interface structure and preset controls, if needed.

## Important Context
- Plate state uses `S.plate`; `makePlateState()` seeds cells, `addCellsToPlate()` adds them, `plateGenome()` resolves genomes, `plateCellMarkup()` renders cells, and `handleAction()` handles interactions.
- Current `plateCellMarkup()` always renders a nucleus and organelles; cell presets will need representation-specific visuals. `cellView()` also assumes a cellular genome and organelles.
- Influenza A and B have eight negative-sense single-stranded RNA segments; HIV infects CD4 T lymphocytes and uses reverse transcriptase.
- Research references: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2263/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/, https://hivinfo.nih.gov/understanding-hiv/fact-sheets/hiv-life-cycle, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4483285/
- Existing uncommitted changes are in `app.js`, `style.css`, `index.html`, and `genesis-latest.jpeg`; no preset changes have been made yet.

## Objective
- Extend GENESIS’s seeded plate with selectable rat, bird, tuna, influenza, and HIV presets, with research-informed educational responses.

## Requirements
- Provide all five as selectable plate presets with accurate, research-grounded explanations.
- Label simplified schematic mechanics as illustrative; distinguish viruses from cells.
- Preserve the DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and *Chlamydomonas*-inspired cell schematic.

## Decisions
- Influenza and HIV are non-cellular viruses: they have no nucleus or organelles and do not divide independently.
- Bird and tuna presets represent nucleated erythrocytes; rat preset represents a hepatocyte, not a mature mammalian red blood cell.
- Virus presets should depict free virions, not host cells or infection progression.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected plate state, rendering, cell observatory, and action-handling code.
- Added `PLATE_PRESETS` definitions in `app.js` for rat hepatocyte, chicken erythrocyte, tuna erythrocyte, influenza A virion, and HIV-1 virion, including educational descriptions, sources, and cellular-versus-virus distinctions.

### Active
- Implement preset selection and representation-aware plate initialization/rendering and educational responses.
- Prevent virus presets from advancing through cell-cycle or cell-division mechanics.
- Verify visuals, interaction behavior, and illustrative-mechanics labels.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Add preset-selection controls and implement loading/initialization for the five `PLATE_PRESETS` in `app.js`.
2. Make plate rendering and `cellView()` representation-specific; viruses should not show cell organelles or cell-state readings.
3. Guard cell advancement, division, and cell-only actions for virus presets.
4. Verify the experience and ensure educational caveats and research links are visible.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Contains `PLATE_PRESETS`, plate state, rendering, observatory view, and action handling.
- `style.css`: Plate and cell visualization styles; add distinct virus and organism styling.
- `index.html`: Add preset controls if appropriate.

## Important Context
- Existing uncommitted changes are in `app.js`, `style.css`, `index.html`, and `genesis-latest.jpeg`; the current work added another uncommitted `app.js` change.
- Relevant simulation functions include `makePlateState()`, `addCellsToPlate()`, `plateGenome()`, `plateCellMarkup()`, `cellView()`, `advancePlateCells()`, and `dividePlateCell()`.
- Virus educational references are embedded in `PLATE_PRESETS`; prior references include https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2263/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/, https://hivinfo.nih.gov/understanding-hiv/fact-sheets/hiv-life-cycle, and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4483285/.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Extend GENESIS’s seeded plate with selectable rat, bird, tuna, influenza, and HIV presets, with accurate, research-grounded educational explanations.

## Requirements
- Provide all five as selectable plate presets with accurate, research-grounded explanations.
- Label simplified schematic mechanics as illustrative; distinguish viruses from cells.
- Preserve the DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and *Chlamydomonas*-inspired cell schematic.

## Decisions
- Influenza and HIV are non-cellular viruses: they have no nucleus or organelles and do not divide independently.
- Bird and tuna presets represent nucleated erythrocytes; rat preset represents a hepatocyte, not a mature mammalian red blood cell.
- Virus presets depict free virions, not host cells or infection progression.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added `PLATE_PRESETS` definitions in `app.js` for rat hepatocyte, chicken erythrocyte, tuna erythrocyte, influenza A virion, and HIV-1 virion, including educational descriptions, sources, and cellular-versus-virus distinctions.

### Active
- Add preset-selection controls and implement loading, initialization, and representation-aware plate rendering.
- Make `cellView()` specific to cells or viruses; viruses should not show cell organelles or cell-state readings.
- Guard cell advancement, division, and cell-only actions for virus presets.
- Verify visuals, interaction behavior, and illustrative-mechanics labels.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Add preset-selection controls in `index.html` and wire selection/loading in `app.js`.
2. Make plate initialization, `plateCellMarkup()`, and `cellView()` reflect cellular versus virion representations.
3. Prevent virus presets from advancing through cell-cycle or cell-division mechanics and disable inappropriate cell-only actions.
4. Verify the experience and ensure educational caveats and research links are visible.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Preset definitions, plate state, rendering, observatory view, and action handling.
- `index.html`: Add preset controls.
- `style.css`: Plate and cell visualization styles; add distinct virus and organism styling.

## Important Context
- Existing uncommitted changes are in `app.js`, `style.css`, `index.html`, and `genesis-latest.jpeg`; the current work added another uncommitted `app.js` change.
- Relevant simulation functions include `makePlateState()`, `addCellsToPlate()`, `plateGenome()`, `plateCellMarkup()`, `cellView()`, `advancePlateCells()`, and `dividePlateCell()`.
- Preset references are embedded in `PLATE_PRESETS`; examples include https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2263/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/, https://hivinfo.nih.gov/understanding-hiv/fact-sheets/hiv-life-cycle, and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4483285/.

## Objective
- Extend GENESIS’s seeded plate with selectable rat, bird, tuna, influenza, and HIV presets, with accurate educational explanations and representation-specific visuals/behavior.

## Requirements
- Provide all five as selectable plate presets with research-grounded explanations and visible sources.
- Clearly label simplified mechanics as illustrative and distinguish viruses from cells.
- Preserve the DNA Codex, researcher progression, periodic table, and *Chlamydomonas*-inspired schematic.

## Decisions
- Influenza and HIV are non-cellular viruses: they have no nucleus or organelles and do not divide independently.
- Bird and tuna presets represent nucleated erythrocytes; rat represents a hepatocyte, not a mature mammalian red blood cell.
- Virus presets depict free virions, not host cells or infection progression.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added `PLATE_PRESETS` in `app.js` for rat hepatocyte, chicken erythrocyte, tuna erythrocyte, influenza A virion, and HIV-1 virion, with descriptions, distinctions, and source links.

### Active
- Add preset-selection controls and wire preset selection/loading in `index.html` and `app.js`.
- Make plate initialization and rendering (`plateCellMarkup()`, `cellView()`) reflect cellular versus virion representations.
- Guard cell advancement/division and cell-only actions for virus presets.
- Verify visuals, interaction behavior, educational caveats, and visible research links.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Add preset controls in `index.html` and selection/loading logic in `app.js`.
2. Implement representation-aware plate state, markup, and observatory details.
3. Prevent virus presets from using cell-cycle/division mechanics and disable inappropriate cell-only actions.
4. Test presets, visuals, behavior, and educational/source visibility.

## Relevant Files
- `app.js`: Preset data, plate state, rendering, observatory view, and action handling.
- `index.html`: Preset controls belong in the app markup.
- `style.css`: Plate and cell visualization styles; add distinct virus and organism styling.

## Important Context
- Uncommitted changes exist in `app.js`, `style.css`, `index.html`, and `genesis-latest.jpeg`; preset definitions are in `app.js`.
- Relevant functions include `makePlateState()`, `addCellsToPlate()`, `plateGenome()`, `plateCellMarkup()`, `cellView()`, `advancePlateCells()`, and `dividePlateCell()`.
- Preset references include https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2263/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3074182/, https://hivinfo.nih.gov/understanding-hiv/fact-sheets/hiv-life-cycle, and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4483285/.
- Existing `cellView()` and `plateCellMarkup()` currently assume cells, including organelles and cell-cycle state; `tick()` calls `advancePlateCells()` unconditionally.
